title: Curiosity Before Expertise
short_teaser: Many discoveries begin with a question, not an answer.
story: Innovators often begin without knowing exactly how something will work. They learn through testing, adjusting, and continuing to explore. Many discoveries begin with a question, not an answer. Curiosity changes an ordinary fact into an invitation. Instead of stopping at what happened, it asks what else might be true, what assumptions may be incomplete, and what becomes visible when we look again. The lasting importance is simple: you do not always need to know everything before you begin.
impact: You do not always need to know everything before you begin. Curiosity loosens the grip of assumptions and creates room for better questions. This matters because the lesson is transferable. It can help someone recognize a pattern, make a more thoughtful choice, or see possibility where they previously saw only a problem.
spark_application: What could you learn by experimenting? Write three questions about something you have been assuming is fixed. Choose the question that opens the most possibility. Afterward, save a short note about what you noticed, what surprised you, or what you may want to revisit.
